lesson.title: The Whole Family of Antiderivatives, in One Expression
lesson.summary: The indefinite integral gathers every antiderivative of a function into a single expression, written as a general formula plus an arbitrary constant.
lesson.body:
In the last chapter you found that f(x) = 3x^2 has more than one antiderivative: x^3 works, but so does x^3 + 5, x^3 - 12, or x^3 plus any other constant. Rather than listing these one at a time, mathematicians write down a single expression that represents the entire family at once. That expression is called the indefinite integral of f.

The indefinite integral of f(x) is written ∫f(x)dx, and by definition it equals F(x) + C, where F is any one antiderivative you found and C stands for an arbitrary constant that can be any real number. The word 'indefinite' signals exactly this: the answer is not one definite function but an entire family of functions, all sharing the same derivative.

This is a direct extension of the idea of an antiderivative. Finding an antiderivative answers the question 'give me one function whose derivative is f.' Finding the indefinite integral answers the broader question 'give me every function whose derivative is f, described in one formula.' The two ideas are tightly linked: you cannot write down an indefinite integral without first knowing how to find at least one antiderivative.

Returning to the worked example from before, f(x) = 3x^2 had antiderivative F(x) = x^3, since d/dx[x^3] = 3x^2. The indefinite integral packages this as ∫3x^2 dx = x^3 + C. To confirm this represents the whole family correctly, differentiate the general expression: d/dx[x^3 + C] = 3x^2 + 0 = 3x^2, which matches f(x) for any choice of C. Whether C is 0, 5, -12, or 1000, the derivative comes out the same, which is exactly why a single formula with a floating constant can stand in for infinitely many individual antiderivatives.
